<pb n="124"/>Even though the nature of the body and the distinctions of the fields and so forth differ, because they have attained equality through the Truth Body <term>dharmakaya</term>, he is said to "abide in the wisdom of the Blessed Buddhas of the past, future, and present." Regarding non-abiding wisdom: because he does not abide in either cyclic existence or nirvana, he is "not abiding in nirvana." That very same state of "abiding at the limit of reality" is what constitutes not abiding in the nirvana of Hearers <term>shravakas</term> and so forth. The "limit of reality" is the perfectly pure suchness <term>tathata</term>, which is itself the Truth Body. To abide in that is called "abiding at the limit of reality." 

Regarding the phrase "abiding on the ground of beholding all sentient beings," the summarized meaning is this: the ground of beholding all sentient beings consists of the three bodies <term>trikaya</term> of the Tathagata. That is to say, since the Tathagata abides in that very reality, perceives the mental continuums of all sentient beings, and teaches the Dharma through the gates of the three vehicles <term>triyana</term> according to their respective inclinations, he is said to "abide" in those three bodies. Thus the scripture states: "The Blessed One, in his Enjoyment Body <term>sambhogakaya</term>, teaches the Dharma of the Great Vehicle <term>mahayana</term> to the noble Avalokiteshvara and other great beings who abide on the ten levels <term>bhumi</term>, and he dwells in the Akanistha realm." This explains how he applies himself to the welfare of beings through the Enjoyment Body. 

He also applies himself to the welfare of beings through the Emanation Body <term>nirmanakaya</term>. As it says in the established treatises: "The Blessed One, in his Emanation Body, perceives the mental continuums of those in the desire realm such as the noble Shariputra and other fortunate ones. By showing the three miracles, he teaches the nature of the Dharma of the Hearer Vehicle according to their inclinations and fortunes, and he abides for as long as cyclic existence lasts." Thus the Emanation Body is also shown to possess that quality. <pb n="125"/> Since the Truth Body is the basis for both, it serves as their cause and is therefore the primary cause. Without it, neither of those two would exist, and thus there would be no performing the welfare of beings. Therefore, it is established that the "ground of beholding all sentient beings" consists of the three bodies of the Tathagata. These are the authentic qualities of the Tathagata. 

The summary verses for this section are:
Continuous form, sentient beings,
The suitability of those activities,
Non-attachment to realms and things,
Perfected abandonment and wisdom.
This practice for the sake of others
Is excellently shown by these words:
Two, six, three, and four;
Six, three, two, and two sets of four.
The body is shown in six ways:
Through the words for basic classification,
Cause, essence, state, and
Perfected activities, it is explained here.
The perfect Teacher, the cause,
The "Thus Gone" <term>tathagata</term> himself,
And his enlightened activity and state;
These are condensed for easy recollection.

The Extensive Commentary on the Noble Recollection of the Buddha, composed by the Master Vasubandhu, is completed. It was translated, edited, and finalized by the Indian scholar Danashila and the chief editor and translator, the monk Paltseg Rakshita.

<note>D3988</note> In the language of India: <term>Ekagatha-bhashya</term>. In the language of Tibet: <term>Explanation of the Single Verse</term>. 

Homage to the All-Knowing One!
O Great Bull among men, a great renunciate like you
Exists not in the god realms nor on this earth.
You are not found in this world, nor in the abode of Vaishravana.
You are not in the supreme palaces of the gods,
Nor in the cardinal or intermediate directions.
Though one circles the vast earth with its mountains and forests,
Where could one ever find your equal?

This verse refers to the time when the Blessed One Shakyamuni was a <pb n="126"/> Bodhisattva. By practicing mindfulness for seven days and nights, he completed the nature of the perfection of diligence. By praising all the perfect qualities of the Blessed One Pushya, he clearly expressed his own unique perfections. 

In that regard, those who are masters of specific fixed locations and are considered supreme in the world include: Brahma in the god realms, the Twins <term>Yama</term>, those of Tushita, those who Delight in Emanation, and the Controllers of Others' Emanations. Regarding the "earth" <term>sa la</term>, because of the connection to the ground, there is Shakra <note>Indra</note> on the peak of Mount Meru. This is one specific location, which is why the text says "supreme palaces." On the northern side of the four tiers of Meru resides the Son of Vaishravana. The phrase "in the directions" refers to the four kings: Vaishravana, Virupaksha, Virudhaka, and Dhritarashtra. The "intermediate directions" refer to the four tiered houses atop Mount Meru where Vajrapani rules. 

These beings are devoid of compassion, abandonment, and wisdom. Since they are not equal in any way to the virtuous results obtained by the Blessed One, how could they possibly be superior to him? Those who are masters of various unfixed locations and are considered "supreme persons" in this world include Vishnu <note>the Destroyer</note>, Ishvara <note>Shiva</note>, and the Cosmic Person <term>Purusha</term>. Since they possess afflictions and suffering, their bodies and minds are not perfectly at peace. Since they are not even equal to the Hearers, what need is there to mention the Blessed One? 

Then there are the Brahmins and Kings who are honored as "supreme persons" because they are adorned with many followers, abundant harvests, and uncommon qualities. Yet, because of their poor intentions and applications, they too are not equal to the Hearers. As for those who have generally attained liberation—the Solitary Buddhas <term>pratyekabuddha</term>, the Hearers, those who dwell in the open air, in charnel grounds, or in forests—the Tathagata has praised these great beings and described them all.
</translation>

<summary>This text concludes Vasubandhu's commentary on the Recollection of the Buddha, explaining the three bodies of a Buddha and their role in helping beings. It then begins a commentary on a single verse of praise, comparing the Buddha's unique qualities to worldly gods and supreme figures.</summary>
<keywords>Tathagata, Trikaya, Dharmakaya, Sambhogakaya, Nirmanakaya, Vasubandhu, Pushya Buddha, Devas, Meru, Shravaka, Liberation</keywords>
